en: Teaching what is unknown,
The learned saint Bakai;
Making the unperceived understood,
The perceptive elder Bakai;
Who had pledged himself to twelve spiritual guides,
The saint sustained by Shai;
Who had received a letter from the caliph,
And a blessing from the prince;
Who was also called a mighty conqueror:
A cloud stirred in the sky,
And to your fierce father Manas
He became a friend at thirty.
If you hear the story of Bakai,
He is the foal of sainthood,
The white hawk of humankind.
The saint who had seen many things,
To your fierce father Manas,
The elder who gave support:
Hardship six months away,
He could perceive and know at once,
The clairvoyant saint.
Your cherished father, the sultan,
That saint Bakai
Led about and made a warrior;
Your fierce father Manas,
He made the equal of warriors' sons.
That elder Bakai,
Your fierce father Manas,
He planted and tended into an orchard;
He built him into a house;
He joined what had broken,
He gathered what had been scattered.
Bakai led your father with him;
They went and struck the Afghans.
Untouched by your father's hand,
How could Margalan have escaped unharmed?
They reached and struck the Afghans;
How could Zhet-Kait have escaped unharmed?
He struck Zhelpinish and took it seven times;
He ravaged India and took it twice.
He struck Ombu and took booty;
Bakai was at his side that day,
Breaking through their midst to make a road.
He seized Kakan and took it three times;
With the eagle Bakai leading the way,
More than that, he struck China and took it four times.
Breaking royal courts, taking booty,
Loading gold coins upon elephants,
With that Bakai beside him,
Your father took a thousand dark-eyed women.
That the gray falcon had not struck,
Not a swan remained unscathed.
That had not heard the fierce battle cry,
Not a people remained untouched.
That the bare spear's point had not touched,
Not a lion remained unscathed.
Akkula and the Blue Tulpar—
Where these two had not trodden,
Not a place remained untouched.
My saint, the lion Bakai,
He is the lion of perfect resourcefulness.
To your father, gone to the other world,
He was the hero who stood as companion.
If what I say is not false,
To your father, Sultan Manas,
He was the lion born an equal.
He finds a way to see in darkness,
Finds the right words in sudden peril.
He does not run out of means and become helpless.
Set that fierce one in the dark
Upon a prowling beast's track—he will not stray.
He is the support to bind about your waist;
He is the renowned lion Bakai.
His blessing enriched the people;
He is a lion like a prophet.
When he said 'Amen,' his prayer
Was accepted—he is that hero.
If you reach Talas alive,
Great Bakai will be your support;
He is the lion who spares nothing for you.
Your fierce Uncle Bakai,
Be sure to find him!
If you scatter, he gathers you together;
Your uncle, the elder Bakai,
If you die, he will see to your rites of faith.
Sovereign Bakai, your tried and trusted one,
Your inheritance from your father Manas.
Your father Manas, the lion,
And Prince Bakai, the panther,
Shared a sheepfold for their flocks,
Shared their meals as companions.
They scouted together;
They seized horses from foreign-tongued folk.
They crushed the Kyzylbash people;
Their fame became known to the people;
They made their women and maidens weep.
The black city of Beijing—
He is the lion Bakai who besieged it.
All who acted as enemies,
He is the lion who went and beat them.
Those who understood his words,
He frightened with his tongue;
The Chinese who did not know the language,
He frightened with his faith.
Sated with blood, hardened by battle,
He earned the name of Bakai the Panther.
He is the one whose fortune is complete;
Your ocean is that hero Bakai.
Let me tell you of Bakai,
If you ask about Bakai,
He nurtured us as a father,
Protected us as a mother.
When I, your bereaved mother,
Had my possessions scattered,
When I fled Talas on foot,
Unable to cross Küyük Pass,
Burning with grief, weeping, unable to walk,
Unable to cross Zhorgo Pass,
Lamenting, weeping, unable to walk...
Bakai arrived, calling out,
Crying, 'Kanykei, my mourning child!'
He gave a letter of command for Bukhara;
To me, your wretched mother,
He gave two swift horses,
Gave six skins of milk,
Spoke good, comforting words,
Saying, 'Go to Bukhara.'
The wether Bakai slaughtered for us,
His reddish, blaze-faced wether—
Until I die, it will not leave my heart,
Nor the deeds of those brute dogs in Talas.
This very year Khan Bakai,
His royal person, must have faded.
His weariness and exhaustion
Must have lasted twelve full years.
At the head of Besh-Tash, a secure summer pasture,
He must have settled in hiding.
Against Abyke and Köbösh,
He must have turned and fought.
He must have earned the name of robber;
Your Bakai must have been disgraced.
For twelve full years,
Great Bakai has herded camels;
When the Blue Tulpar could no longer walk,
Great Bakai herded them on foot.
Your heroic Uncle Bakai—
If you do not go this year,
With his beard grown white,
When it is time to depart,
Your uncle, herding camels,
Is ready to die this very year.
An old coat upon his body,
Hide trousers upon his legs,
His black beard grown white,
This very year Khan Bakai
Is at the hour of death.
The horse he rode beneath him,
The maned red one, the marked gray one,
The shining Blue Tulpar—
If you ask about its former days,
It was not yet bobtailed then,
Had not yet acquired an ill name.
If you ask about it now,
Herding camels, its saddle never taken off,
Unable to graze freely and crop the grass,
Without sleep on summer days,
Without peace on winter days,
Khan Bakai's Blue Tulpar
Must have gained the name of Bobtailed Gray;
This year it must have gained an ill name.
Hardship and misfortune must have struck it;
This year it must have become mangy.
Losing its mane and tail,
It must have come to be called a bobtailed horse.
This very year the Blue Tulpar
Must have been disgraced indeed.
Losing the name of Blue Tulpar,
It must have gained the name of Bobtailed Gray.
Khan Bakai upon its back,
Agitated and wandering, must have faded.
If you do not go this year,
He must be on the point of death.
My poor child, when you come near,
He will not recognize you.
The reason he will not know you—
His eyes are full of pus;
His chest has begun to rattle.
Life has fled; he is not counted among the living,
Yet he has not died and lies in no grave.
'Fierce Manas, do not die!' he cries;
Bakai weeps and sobs,
Wasting away in these days.
'Beard of a wretch,
You have lived so long without dying!' he says,
Tearing at his own beard,
Plucking it out in these days.
'When will my wish be granted?
When will my orphan come?' he cries,
Howling in these days.
When Bakai bends over,
The flesh at his kneecaps parts;
When Bakai stoops,
His testicles are fully exposed.
His fur cap worn out, bareheaded,
Without a shirt, naked,
He is your poor Khan Bakai.
Meet him and become his companion;
He is your tiger, Bakai.
He is the hero who finds a way,
In place of your father, Khan Manas,
He is the lion who will support you.
Let me leave this here;
Again, my son, another tale—
Let me begin farther back.
Your cord-father Bölökbay—
Let me tell you of him.
The lame smith Bölökbay,
A star stirred in the heavens;
Your Bölök and David
Were friends unto the Last Judgment.
Putting all his skill into his work,
Taking counsel with David,
He made precious things.
Your father Manas, the lion,
Revealed his sacred worth;
A thousand young mares from his herds
He had given as his portion,
And made him khan of the treasury.
For your lordly, fierce father Manas,
He prepared his swords;
Gathering all the spears,
He made ready against the enemy.
Girding his waist firmly with gold,
Let me tell your Bölök's early story:
He was born in broad Crimea below.
Manas had the land searched,
The great felt cap, large as a yurt roof-cover—
He had brought from the hero Shuutu.
For your father, Sultan Manas,
He forged Zulpukor and brought it into being;
He made all his equipment ready.
Making Talas his homeland,
Completing all the equipment,
The lame smith Bölökbay
Made your father Manas strong.
The heroic smith Bölökbay
Came and settled in Talas,
Became a companion to your father Manas alone.
When your father died,
When the six villains came and divided the treasury,
He fought with gunfire for sixty days.
Divided, he was struck down.
Your father's forty companions
And the six leaders united;
Bölökbay lost the treasury.
The treasury of gold and silver,
